title: Data Science Fundamentals
headline: See the system behind the statistic.
overview: Examined how data, models and operational decisions fit together. The hospital-discharge case and simplified-data exercise developed a habit of questioning the population, aggregation and decision context before choosing an algorithm.
work: My written reflection used CT-scanner demand to show how aggregated physician activity can hide differences in case mix and workload. A useful representation must preserve the information needed for the decision.
insight: Segment the data before interpreting a headline average; a relationship can change when relevant groups are examined separately.
application: Healthcare operations: assess patient flow and resource demand with appropriate segmentation.

title: Thinking About Risk and Uncertainty Through Probability Distributions
headline: Make uncertainty part of the decision.
overview: Used probability distributions to represent uncertain demand and connect predictive information to prescriptive decisions. The coursework moved from a single expected value toward the range of outcomes a manager must plan for.
work: Completed the patient-booking exercise in Codio, applying predictive data to a prescriptive model. The original hosted notebook is not exportable; this page records the task, concepts and verified assessment result.
insight: Capacity decisions should account for variability as well as average demand. Pooling can change the risk profile when demands are not perfectly correlated.
application: Clinic scheduling: compare booking policies against both utilization and service reliability.

title: Correlation
headline: Understand what moves together—and why it matters.
overview: Explored relationships between variables, including how covariance affects a combined portfolio and how correlation supports initial investigation of business data.
work: Completed the coding assignment on analyzing data for a prescriptive model. The exercises connected measured relationships to portfolio and business decisions without treating association as proof of causation.
insight: Two individually variable assets or workloads can produce a more stable combination when their movements differ. The benefit depends on the joint behavior.
application: Operations planning: examine whether loads, failures or demand streams peak together.

title: Clustering
headline: Turn heterogeneous customers into useful segments.
overview: Studied clustering as a way to discover structure without labeled outcomes. Airline customer segmentation provided a practical setting for considering what makes a cluster meaningful to a business.
work: Completed the K-means coding assignment and exercises on normalization, algorithm components and clustering tradeoffs. The work emphasized choosing comparable features and interpreting groups beyond their numerical labels.
insight: Feature scaling can change the distance calculation and therefore the clusters. A statistically compact cluster still needs an operational interpretation.
application: Service design: segment usage patterns to tailor support, capacity and customer offerings.

title: Linear Regression: Part One
headline: Explain a model in language a decision maker can use.
overview: Interpreted a house-price regression and examined the treatment of unusual observations. Two submitted analyses translated statistical output into recommendations and limitations.
work: The housing memo discussed a supplied model with R² = 0.768 and construction quality, living area, garage area and basement area as predictors. The mortgage-points analysis recommended checking unusual records against their source before exclusion.
insight: A good fit does not establish causation. Outlier thresholds are screening tools; unusual but valid cases may contain important information.
application: Property and operational forecasting: document variable meaning, uncertainty and data-cleaning decisions.

title: Linear Regression: Part Two
headline: Test whether a model generalizes.
overview: Extended linear regression from interpretation to validation. The module examined how training fit, statistical significance and out-of-sample performance answer different questions.
work: Completed a Codio portfolio assignment using multiple regression on the diabetes case. The emphasis was on building and evaluating a prediction model rather than relying only on in-sample fit.
insight: A more complex model can fit the training data better while making poorer predictions on new observations. Evaluation must reflect the intended use.
application: Operational forecasting: reserve unseen data and compare candidate models against a clear baseline.

title: Logistic Regression
headline: Connect classification errors to business value.
overview: Applied logistic regression to loan repayment and interpreted the consequences of classification errors. The executive memo considered both predictive quality and a lending decision.
work: The submitted LendingClub case memo reported approximately 77% test accuracy using a 70/30 split. The assignment scenario estimated profit increasing from about $5.6 million to $6.1 million. These are course-case estimates, not realized client results.
insight: Accuracy alone is insufficient. False approvals and false denials carry different costs, so thresholds and confusion-matrix outcomes matter.
application: Decision support: pair classification metrics with explicit business costs and human review.

title: Collaborative Filtering
headline: Learn preferences from incomplete ratings.

insight: Observed ratings are selective. Sparsity, cold-start users and popularity effects should shape the interpretation of recommendation quality.
application: Product personalization: recommend useful next actions while retaining exploration and user choice.

title: Optimization: Part One
headline: Express a management decision as a solvable model.
overview: Formulated decision variables, objectives and constraints for advertising, production and coal procurement. Three assignments developed the translation from a business narrative to a mathematical model.
work: The submitted coal model records a total supply cost of $73,267,500 and an average of about $59.81 per ton. Advertising coverage was expressed as explicit audience constraints. Reviewed numerical extracts are available below.
insight: Units and constraint direction deserve as much attention as the objective. A solver optimizes the model it receives, including any formulation errors.
application: Procurement and capacity allocation: make tradeoffs and feasibility explicit before comparing options.

title: Optimization: Part Two
headline: Find the bottleneck before funding more capacity.
overview: Used the Craft Studio Furnishings case to connect an optimal production mix with resource utilization and a management recommendation.
work: My submitted memo recommends 0 table chairs, 4 easy chairs, 20 love seats, 10 coffee tables and 10 end tables per week, for a modeled weekly contribution of $2,316. Frame manufacturing and finishing are fully utilized; stretching has spare capacity.
insight: Additional capacity creates value only where it relaxes a binding limitation within the relevant sensitivity range. The recommendation must change when the inputs change.
application: Manufacturing and service operations: prioritize investments using marginal value, then re-solve the model.

title: Optimization: Part Three
headline: Combine demand prediction with pricing decisions.
overview: Built a demand model using current price, two lagged prices and seasonal terms, then used it to recommend an eight-week pricing schedule for an amusement-park case.
work: The submitted analysis explains the negative current-price coefficient and positive lagged-price effects. It also proposes price-change limits, additional demand drivers and a controlled field experiment to evaluate actual value.
insight: Optimized revenue estimated by the same model is not independent evidence of improvement. A prospective experiment is needed to test business impact.
application: Commercial planning: use forecast-driven optimization with price guardrails and ongoing recalibration.

insight: Partial-dependence patterns describe a fitted model. They should not automatically be interpreted as causal effects, especially when features are correlated.
application: Operations forecasting: connect interpretable model behavior to staffing and capacity planning.

title: Nonlinear Models for Regression and Classification: Ensemble Learning
headline: Look beyond a strong headline accuracy.
overview: Explored ensemble learning and assessed a loan-default classifier. The written submission considered feature importance and challenged a potentially misleading evaluation result.
work: My analysis reported approximately 83.4% test accuracy, with FICO and installment among the leading features. It also flagged a reported 50% ROC-AUC for investigation and recommended using predicted probabilities and a confusion matrix.
insight: A high accuracy score can hide failure on the minority class. Feature-importance scores describe the fitted model and do not prove causation.
application: Risk modeling: evaluate ranking, calibration and class-specific errors before choosing a decision threshold.

title: Fairness and Bias Issues in Data-Driven Predictions
headline: Evaluate who bears the cost of an error.
overview: Examined representation, measurement and automation bias through a facial-recognition analysis and a lending-model board memo.
work: In the FairBank course case, both groups had a 16% overall error rate, yet false-denial rates were 30% and 18%. My memo recommended subgroup evaluation, better measures of repayment ability and ongoing monitoring.
insight: Equal overall error rates can conceal materially different harms. Model evaluation must reflect the affected people and the consequence of each error.
application: AI governance: define subgroup checks, escalation rules and meaningful human accountability.

insight: An unusual behavior is not necessarily fraudulent. Thresholds, drift monitoring and a review process are essential to protect legitimate users.
application: Trust and safety: use learned representations to prioritize investigation with appropriate review.

headline: Trace the calculation from input to prediction.
overview: Connected network mathematics to implementation through a hand-worked forward pass and a heart-disease classification exercise.

insight: A pre-activation value and an activated probability are different quantities. Naming each stage makes implementation errors easier to identify.
application: Model review: verify simple calculations before trusting a larger training pipeline.

title: Natural Language Processing: Part One
headline: Distinguish contextual similarity from meaning.
overview: Explored word representations and sentiment classification. A written analysis tested whether vector similarity distinguishes synonyms from antonyms.
work: My embedding experiment found high/low similarity of 0.8511, compared with good/excellent at 0.8062. I also completed the IMDB sentiment-classification portfolio assignment in Codio.
insight: Words with opposite meanings may appear in similar contexts and therefore have nearby vectors. A downstream task needs context beyond similarity alone.
application: Clinical and operational text: evaluate semantic errors before using extracted language in decisions.

title: Interpretability and Causality in Models
headline: Keep a complex signal accountable at the decision layer.
overview: Proposed incorporating third-party telematics into an insurance pricing model while preserving an understandable final decision process.
work: My submitted paper recommends a separate behavioral-risk model feeding a simpler pricing layer, with checks for exposure, identity, sensor quality, consent, subgroup effects and drift.
insight: Interpretability does not itself establish causality. A two-stage design still needs causal assumptions, appropriate validation and careful treatment of selection and confounding.
application: Decision architecture: separate rich representation learning from an auditable decision layer.

headline: Choose the right level of automation for the decision.
overview: Applied an AI use-case taxonomy to alarm management, inventory and accounting, then developed a clinical-documentation implementation proposal.

insight: Automation should follow the structure of the input and the consequence of the output. Accountability remains an explicit design choice.
application: PAN Enterprise: develop governed clinical-documentation assistance with human approval and auditability.
